utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, you can proceed to call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number, IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Brdjanin, good afternoon to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. I can hear you and I understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. General Talic, good afternoon to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. I can hear you in a language that I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, General Talic. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner, assisted by case manager Denise Gustin. Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you. Thank you. Appearances for Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman. I'm here with my co-counsel Milan Trbojevic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Trbojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Milan Trbojevic. Thank you. And our assistant Marela Jevtovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And good afternoon to you. And appearances for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours. I am Natasha Ivanovic-Fauveau. I represent General Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And good afternoon to you. And good afternoon to you, Dr. Sabanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. The usher will give you the solemn declaration. And if you could kindly read it out again once more, hoping that this will be the last time you're doing that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any preliminaries before we proceed with the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I thought Your Honour was proceeding with the witness. I can deal with it and it's probably better dealt with when the witness is finished, before the next witness comes in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Korner. Mr. Ackerman, you may proceed or resume your cross-examination of the witness. Dr. Sabanovic, Mr. Ackerman will be continuing his cross-examination of you. Yesterday, Mr. Ackerman, you were in the process of referring the witness, I think if I remember well, to document P754.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah. That will be next, although I've got one other little thing -- two other little things I need to kind of revisit or clear up before I get there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The first thing I'd like to look at is DB86. I'd like the usher to bring it by me and then I'll send it on over to the ELMO. Okay. Take it over to the ELMO, please. Cross-examined by Mr. Ackerman: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, I have Exhibit DB86 back on the ELMO where you can see it. And my question is: Do you see the infirmary on there where you worked? Is it represented on that drawing?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I think it is here, in front of us, of this fence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Dr. Sabanovic, we need to put it on the ELMO and you need to indicate the spot on the ELMO so that we can follow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You think that is the --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Would you just put the letter "I" there with your initials next to it, please.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You have written an "A" it likes like and you put your initials there and that's fine. Okay. Thank you. On your first day of testimony, June 3rd, at -- it's on page 60 of the transcript -- you were referring to photograph number 8. And I guess we ought to get P807 over to the ELMO so we can look at it, because it might be important to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And put it so that we can see photograph number 8, please, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you'll see the photograph of a white building with a red roof there. Underneath it says "infirmary" in English. And you told us the other day, I believe, at page 60 of the transcript that that was the infirmary --

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And that is the building you identified as the infirmary, and also it contained there in the back the isolation cell; correct?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that wouldn't be the infirmary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this description here is wrong then. If that's -- if that says "infirmary" there underneath that --

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- that's incorrect. Do you see on any of these pictures, do you see --

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This isn't the infirmary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. On any of these picture, do you see the infirmary? You can look over -- look over at the document that's on the ELMO so you can see every picture and tell me if you see the infirmary. Just look at the document itself. If you do, what number is it?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first infirmary was here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have to put it back on the ELMO and point to it now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which was the first infirmary, or where was the first infirmary, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You're pointing to photograph number 6, the administration building; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then do you see any other one?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The infirmary was there at the beginning too. But I don't understand these matters very well --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't need to look at the map. Just look at the photos.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see another photo that has the later infirmary on it?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see it here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we went through this in chief. And I'm not sure what the relevance is, however, it's the difference between the word "infirmary" and "hospital." If Your Honours looks at the transcript --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, let's solve it in a very simple manner. I mean, I appreciate what you say, Ms. Korner. Look at photo number 8, Dr. Sabanovic, please. Look at photo number 8.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I can see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You were shown that photo before, two days ago. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you tell us according to you now what is shown in that photo, what building that was or that is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This building here is the hospital. And there was a horse stables there. And this is where the patients would have beds. There were about 30 to 40 of them, and this is the entrance. And here behind, this is the gate to the isolation cell. And there was also an entrance where they would take -- which they would use to take in goods from the Red Cross, et cetera. So the hospital is one thing and the infirmary is another thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So -- one moment, Mr. Ackerman. Let's clear this from our -- from our table straight away. So you are telling us that to you, there is a difference between an infirmary and a hospital. And indeed there is. This was the hospital, according to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Where was this hospital in place? Where was the infirmary? Or was there an infirmary at the same time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Where was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hospital was created before. It was in the command where the police was. I've already said that. And at the same time, in the command there was a place which used to be a slaughterhouse, and that was renovated and they made this -- this hospital. You can't see it here. And this is an infirmary. There was an area behind the stables, behind the kitchen where we would eat, and that's the area where there is an entrance leading to the place where the seriously sick were lying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know if your mind is clear after this explanation, Mr. Ackerman, but you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to have the witness now again look at DB86, Your Honour, because I obviously asked the question improperly. I need to ask it properly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I've got Exhibit DB86 back on the ELMO again. And tell me now if you see the hospital on that drawing.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it should be here, this part here, which is drawn, behind this kitchen. Just here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's --

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's where the hospital should be, and this is where the infirmary should be, because the command building was here to the left. That's where the command should be, where the infirmary used to be, and that should be the premises which are now used for the infirmary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So the hospital is basically missing from this drawing. It hasn't been drawn in.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can't see it here. You can see very little here. It's probably here. Something has been drawn which is a low sort of structure, but not very well. I don't know who drew it. I don't know whether it's been done very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That low structure, could you just put some kind of a designation there. And I understand that that is the area where you're saying the hospital was but it's not representative of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He can put an "H."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That should be the place. And this should be the area. But the first part could have been the place, the one that we were just looking at, where I said that the infirmary was located. That seems to fit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I appreciate that interruptions actually sometimes delay matters even more, but I do ask given that this witness is anxious to get away what any of this has to do with the case for Mr. Brdjanin. And we could go on forever with whether the drawing is accurate or the photograph or the descriptions. But I really do ask what's the relevance of this to Mr. Brdjanin's case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman. What's the relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Brdjanin is charged with responsibility for a large number of things that happened in the Krajina and one of the things that he's charged with is things that happened at this very camp, and so it's very relevant to his case. That's why I'm doing this. I wouldn't be doing it if I didn't think it was worth doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. But you haven't explained the proper relevance, I mean of the questions that you are directing at the witness at this present moment and that you have been insisting upon since yesterday. I mean, the - the precise location of the infirmary and the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It has a great deal to do with witness credibility, both this witness and previous witnesses, which I would prefer to reserve for argument at the appropriate time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, please where you think that the hospital was, put an "H" and your initials. And Mr. Ackerman, I invite you to proceed, to ask the witness some other question which is more relevant to the treatment of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is just a formality. What we're doing is just a formality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, Dr. Sabanovic, let us decide whether it's just a formality or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You've put an "H" in the area that you say this hospital with you located.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I'm now finished with this document. And thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us your first day of testimony at page 60 that you started sleeping at some point in the hospital building; correct?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that I started that. I started in the stables and then in the hospital. The hospital wasn't there straight away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. I've not worded my question properly or something. There was a point where you started sleeping in the hospital building; correct?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember whether that was before or after you had been registered by the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, about that time. I don't know exactly, but by the time we sorted everything out, we sorted that area out and that happened later on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is it your answer that it was about the time you were registered by the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was, and maybe even afterwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Maybe afterwards. Okay. I'd like you to look now at Exhibit P754. And what we had talked about yesterday with regard to Emir Mulalic had to do with some information that the German authorities apparently had received that you had reanimated him at Manjaca, which you told the German authorities and told us was not the case. If you look at this newspaper article - and this is Prosecution Exhibit 754, sir - if you look at this newspaper article, you'll see a box down to the -- just to the right of the two photographs. The headline is [B/C/S spoken]. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cadjavica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Cadjavica. In that article, it talks about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, one moment. Because I'm not that sure that we have -- 754. What we have is --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I'm sorry. I shouldn't -- I was asking him without the microphone. But is this article translated?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think what His Honour is worried about and what I can't find is where is the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is some confusion. 754 I have photocopies of two different newspaper articles. The first one, which I don't think has anything to do with what you're asking the witness now, has as a title [B/C/S spoken]. And this is what has been indicated as Exhibit 754. Then it continues, and there seems to be another article, completely different and by a different person.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's all here, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Is it the translation that's headed, the article "Interviews with prisoners from Manjaca"?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, no, it isn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, in that case, that's what I mean. There are a number of articles and a number of translations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is -- is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's called --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it the newspaper -- page from the newspaper where there are two photos of two individuals --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Skin and bones.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then to the right there is the box --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is that the box you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And this is also 754? Because --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's -- according to my records, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we put it on the ELMO, both the English and the B/C/S, please. And then we'll all see where we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 754 goes on and on and on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And what's -- okay. And what's the translation, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the translation is headed "Truth about death camp 7, the wheel of crime."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the very last paragraph of that says "Crime in Cadjavica."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would that get us there? Your Honours now have what we're referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. But the thing is it needs to be indicated properly because all this seems to be document 754 -- Exhibit 754. And there are still other cuttings from other newspapers coming up in the same document, before and after. So let's -- for -- to be precise, we are referring to the page which is marked with the number "00491525" in the B/C/S version and page "01107782" in the English --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's exactly correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- version. Okay. So there are at least -- later on if we need to refer to this, we'll be able to. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, the only thing I want to bring to your attention is just very -- that very short article. And I'm not going to read the whole article. But it indicates that a person by the name of Emir Mulalic was killed by a Dane Kajtaz and a Ducan Saovic while they were being escorted from Manjaca at the well-known Chetnik stronghold of Cadjavica in a forest near the Gaj motel. My question is: Was there more than one Emir Mulalic that you knew of who was confined at Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And what is written there is not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Dr. Sabanovic, that was not the question asked from you. As far as you can say, was there only one Emir Mulalic or more than one person with that same name in Manjaca? If you know the answer, then tell us. If you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just one person. You --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one. That's for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm certain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. You've got your answer now, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My next question, sir, is similar: Were there two people in Manjaca named Omer Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there was only one person named Omer Filipovic who you gave testimony about having died at Manjaca; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And according to your testimony, at page 68 you and Dr. Derviskadic were called to the isolation cell at about 10.00 on a particular morning, where you found the dead body of Mr. Filipovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's -- we didn't find it. The police took us there to the place where the man was lying dead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you actually saw the body of Omer Filipovic in that isolation cell.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that one of the nights that you had slept in the hospital? Were you taken there straight from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the same building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that night while you were sleeping in that same building, did you hear any screams or noises or anything like that coming from the isolation cell?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. It was a nightly occurrence practically. But that man, knowing what he looked like before that, there wasn't -- one couldn't really expect to hear his screams, because when I saw him there he was only about 30 per cent of his appearance, of his body physique at the time when he was healthy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I take it the answer is you did not hear screams from that isolation cell during that night as you were sleeping in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did Dr. Derviskadic indicate to you that he had heard any -- any noises like that during the night?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not deaf, and as far as I know Dr. Derviskadic is not deaf either. We slept in the same place. I repeat, one could hear screams every night, but I do not recall that one could hear anything that night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you told us that when you got to the isolation cell you saw in there a fire extinguisher that had blood upon it and it was clear to you that he had been killed with that fire extinguisher, crushed to some extent with it; correct?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement to the German authorities, doctor -- and I'll ask the Prosecutor to give those back to you, both of your statements, because we're going to refer to them. You were asked about Omer Filipovic -- and I think it's on page 14, but I'm not certain, of the B/C/S version. I don't think so. There it is. It's on page -- it's on page 15, sir, about halfway down. It begins with: [B/C/S spoken] Are you going to look at it or not, or did I just waste my time looking for it?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't need it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The translation -- the English version says this: "Dr. Derviskadic and I found Omer Filipovic dead in the isolation cell one day. After we had been registered by the International Red Cross. It might have been in the morning that we found Omer Filipovic. We were supposed to check whether Omer Filipovic was really dead. I was not able to examine him at the time and therefore cannot tell you what other injuries he had suffered; therefore I cannot tell you the exact cause of his death. However, I assume that he died as a result of mistreatment." Now, is that what you told the German authorities?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Technically it is so poor that I really have no comment. I have no comment, believe it or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I really didn't ask you for a comment. I simply asked you if that's what you told the German authorities. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this must have been literal. But that is not how it was said, no. Simply no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's nothing in that statement that I have that you gave to the German authorities that mentions anything about finding a fire extinguisher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you, Mr. Ackerman. Please refer to the first of these statements, according to my records at least, page 12 to be precise, with the number at the top 02004446, the third full paragraph. "One day an MP told Dr. Derviskadic and I to come with him. We were told to go to the isolation cell and get Omer Filipovic, because he was dead. When I entered the cell which was 2 metres wide by 3 metres long, I saw Omer lying on his back on the concrete floor. He was dead and covered in blood. There was a fire extinguisher near him and the bottom of it was covered in blood."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: "It was clear to me that Omer had died a violent death and that the fire extinguisher had been used to kill him."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour the refer --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You're looking at a different statement, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour's referring to the ICTY statement and that came after the German.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I see. I see, I see.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The German interview was the first in time, the ICTY statement was taken thereafter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Yes, you may proceed with your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I could find nowhere in your statement to the German authorities where you mention anything about a fire extinguisher. Did you tell them about a fire extinguisher?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. It's very short. And these ones here -- I mean, this was translated in such a muddled way that I repeat, I could never take such things into consideration and translate them in this way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you deny that you told the German authorities with regard to Omer Filipovic "I cannot tell you the exact cause of his death"?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. I'm sorry. That's a misrepresentation. The doctor is not denying anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, he can answer that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I deny --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... question to answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. But the whey it's being put, he didn't deny it. If he's being asked whether -- do you deny it, that's a different matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner is right. Rephrase your question, Mr. Ackerman, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The statement that I have from the German authorities reads as follows, sir: "Therefore I cannot tell you the exact cause of his death. However, I assume that he died as a result of mistreatment." Are you saying that that is not true and that that is not what you told the German police?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It has not been translated as I said it. There is a number of things -- there are a number of things here which are not translated properly and did not reflect exactly what I had said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is it your answer that you did not say that?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I did not say it. I explained it. Just like I said to the authorities here, how they translated it. I never read it. I'm not reading it now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you do --

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the truth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You do recognise that I'm giving you the opportunity to read it now, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But there's no reason for me to do it when I know it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that's your position. It says further down: "I examined Omer Filipovic alive for the last time 15 or 16 days before I saw his body." You now say that that's also not correct and you did not say that to the German authorities, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you first. There are few of those whom I did not examine in Manjaca, and I said that 15 days earlier Omer Filipovic was lying in a corner all by himself, nobody could come near him. And I examined everybody. Now you want me after ten years the examinations, several thousand people. I do not know them -- I was Dr. Sabanovic. Others were inmates. How could I know all these people? I don't even know those people who come from my area and had left abroad. Therefore, I don't know who is it -- who was it there that -- whom I did not examine. It wasn't yesterday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And there is also statements to the effect that he was examining something between 100 and 200 inmates every day. So I think that is important to keep in mind, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not asking you to remember back ten years. I'm only asking you to remember back to December of 2000 or February of 2001, when you spoke to the investigator from the Office of the Prosecutor. That's as far back as I want you to remember right now. And isn't it true that you said to the investigator from the Office of the Prosecutor, page 12 of your statement: "In my previous statement, I mentioned that I had examined Omer alive for the last time 15 to 16 days before I saw his body. This is not accurately stated. I never examined his body. I only saw him after he was returned to the stable." That's what you told the Prosecutor just a few months ago; correct?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is impossible. How could his body be returned to the stable? Excuse me. To return a dead man to the stable, I don't understand it. And the one who wrote this and said this, well, it's not that I'm denying it is impossible. It's incomprehensible. Living people are brought into the stable and dead men are taken out from the stable. And from the solitary -- from the isolation cell the dead body was taken directly to Banja Luka. What stable?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, one of two things is happening. You're either not listening or my questions are not being translated properly. So what I want you to do and what I'm going --

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm listening carefully.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what I'm going to ask you to do, because you're -- you're not answering the questions I'm asking you for some reason. One is that you're not listening, or two, they're not being translated properly. So I want you to look at your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. I want you to look at the statement. You get the statement and look at it, the one you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No need.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object. I think this is getting to badgering the witness. It's clear to see Your Honours have a copy of the statement. What he said to the German authorities and what he said to the investigator. And I think we spent enough time on it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Korner is right, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, if he's going to be a witness here, Your Honour, and I ask him proper questions, he should answer it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. But I think two paragraphs -- the relevant paragraphs are there. I mean, the Chamber will withdraw its conclusions. But it can't allow a situation to develop which almost becomes, I would dare say, almost even a harassment. I mean, it's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I just want to object to being cut off from cross-examination which I think is appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You will be cut off if necessary, Mr. Ackerman. Otherwise you know that usually I don't cut you off, neither you or anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And he should probably look at a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you probably come from a jurisdiction where what you're doing now is customary. I come from a jurisdiction where this is not allowed. I am permitting you to go ahead, but there are limits.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you were talking in your direct examination about the death of Esad Bender. And at page 69 of your testimony with regard to his death, you gave the following answer: "It was a violent death. He was covered in blood around his mouth and nose." Let me see if I'm looking at the right one. I may not be looking at the right one. Yes, I am. "The fire extinguisher next to him was also bloodstained in the area where he was hit, and that was around his chest. And that is how we were given a blanket to wrap him in and carry him out."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think that's Filipovic, Your Honour. I think I'm reading the wrong part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's my recollection as well, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, here it is. I've found it. I've found it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With regard to Mr. Bender -- with regard to Mr. Bender, you've said this.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With regard to his death. That is a -- this is on page 70: "That is a violent death. I did that, and I was an expert witness in a district court in Banja Luka before the war. I did the post-mortems. I did exhumations. And it was clear as daylight to me. And every word I'm saying here is gospel truth. He died a violent death." And that's what you told this Chamber during your testimony; correct?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement that you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor -- I'm on page 12 of the English version. The third paragraph up from the bottom you talk both Mr. Bender. You said you had examined him a few times, noticed that he had bruises on his body. You can't remember if you examined him on his arrival to the camp, that there were about 800 people in the same stable the day he died. And then you said this: "I cannot say if Esad's condition worsened during his time in the camp." Correct?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no worsening of the state. That man was all covered in bruises, beaten, beaten, beaten. What worsening of his state?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't know. Those are your words.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The man died. The man died of the injuries. And -- and you can think what you like. You're entitled to it. I'm not saying anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you last speak with Judge Draganovic?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. What do you mean? Of late or ...?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yeah. Recently. When did you last speak to him?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. Talked -- he's a very serious case. He had one of his legs amputated. He's a diabetic. He's often brought to the hospital, and that is it. And we were talking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Dr. Sabanovic. We're talking of a different person. The person that Mr. Ackerman is asking you about -- look at me, please -- is Judge -- Judge Draganovic, the president of the court in Sanski Most, who we have seen here very much in one piece. We can't tell if he is diabetic or not, but he certainly had his two legs and he's definitely not the person that you were mentioning a few minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm told the translation was wrong, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Even the translation is wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think we're having some very serious translation problems today, because he's not answering any questions that I'm asking and I think he's trying to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question, Mr. -- Dr. Sabanovic is this: When did you last speak with Judge Draganovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it could have been a month, a month and a half ago. And I talked with him about his mother. She is a diabetic. She is seriously ill, and we talked about that a number of times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Now we are definitely talking of the same person, Mr. Ackerman, and you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I want to -- I want to stop these proceedings until we get some translators who can translate properly, because it's not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. But first you have to show me where the problem lies.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Apparently almost every question. All you have to do is look at his answers that have nothing to do with my questions, and it's pretty obvious that they're not being translated to him properly and therefore he's giving me answers that have nothing to do with him because he doesn't know what I'm asking him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not necessarily, Mr. Ackerman. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I am very concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. So am I. But when I have proof of what you're alleging, then I will take action but not before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, the proof was in the last question. Obviously it was translated to him that somebody totally different from Judge Draganovic--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But tell me how it was translated to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I wish I knew.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I mean rather than spending time -- both Mr. Ackerman -- he has two co-counsel who understand the language. If there's a fault in the translation, no doubt they can alert him. And Madam Fauveau speaks the language in any event. But I am concerned that we are wasting an awful lot of time on what seem to me particularly do not go to the heart of Mr. Ackerman's case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Proceed, please, Mr. Ackerman. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you speak with Judge Draganovic at all about his having testified here at this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you spoken to anyone about his testimony here at this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you speak to anybody about anyone's testimony at this Tribunal within the last two weeks? You could probably remember that.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Why would I talk about it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you speak to any representative of the AID office in Sarajevo or Sanski Most or any other location in Bosnia-Herzegovina about your testimony here?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only when they would invite me, when I was to come here. Otherwise, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Be precise. Who did you speak to? Because the question was a direct one. Did you speak to any representative of the AID office in Sarajevo or Sanski Most or any other location in Bosnia-Herzegovina about your testimony here? You're saying "only when they would invite me, when I was to come here." Who invited you and who did you speak to? That's what Mr. Ackerman wants to know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With a man called -- whose first name is Zijo. I don't know his last name -- who works in Sanski Most and who informs me where do I have to go and when do I have to go there. That is all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This is quite distressing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But this is what he's telling us, that he spoke with someone called Zijo, if I get it right here. I don't know his last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You can bet big money that it's our friend Zijad Ibric and what is he doing inviting Prosecution witnesses --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Your Honour, if we're going to have this discussion, we'll have it in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are mentioning a name that the witness did not mention.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Mr. Ackerman is perfectly entitled to put direct questions but not make comments of that nature and speeches. If he wants to suggest to the witness that it was Zijad Ibric then by all means suggest it. And then perhaps he might like to ask what discussion there was between him and Zijad Ibric, rather than this cloud of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you are right, Mr. Ackerman -- Ms. Korner. Mr. Ackerman, you are free to put a direct question to the witness, mentioning the person -- name of the person that you have referred to a minute ago and ask whether he has met with this person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it Zijad Ibric that talked to you?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many times did you speak with Zijad Ibric?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As many times as was necessary. When investigating judges came to Sanski Most or when I was to come here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you give statements to Zijad Ibric, written statements?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you give written statements to investigative judges?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those from The Hague and in Germany, if they are investigating judges.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you discuss the testimony that you would give here with Mr. Zijad Ibric?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did Zijad Ibric tell you when he contacted you with regard to coming here to be a witness?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that I needed a passport and a new one at that, so that I changed the passport two or three days before I came here, and that he would let me know when they came to take me to The Hague. That was that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When they came. Do you know who "they" were?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are people from the United Nations. A man from the United Nations who came to fetch me. I was working at the time, and he went there and he brought me here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if Mr. Ackerman wants to hear evidence from the VWS about how witnesses arrive here, then we'll call somebody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think it's necessary, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we already have -- I'll take this up at a later time, but I'm becoming concerned about this and I want to raise it but I don't want to do it now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you speak with anyone from any detainees association about the testimony you would give here?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us in your transcript at page -- in your testimony at page 71 of the transcript -- you said: "There was a judge who was --" referring to your time in Manjaca, sir. "There was a judge who was called out two or three times and luckily he did not respond. He certainly would not have lived to see the day." Do you know who that was?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it the case that people were free to -- to not respond when they were called out?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that you had actually treated Lieutenant Colonel Popovic and the person called Spaga, the warden, for their medical problems; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you told us that they had on occasion asked you to drink whiskey with them; true?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there were in fact some occasions when you did that, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement to the German authorities, sir, you were asked a question which you described as a fairy tale. Do you remember that question that they asked you which you called a fairy tale?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you be more specific, Mr. Ackerman? Because he --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm trying to save some time. Your Honour. If we can save some time by doing it this way, we will. If not, I'll have to be a lot more specific. But he might remember, if he doesn't then I can remind him of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about a fairy tale.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. The investigator said to you that they had a statement which said that Mr. Bender, Esad Bender, was carried on a blanket by four prisoners into shed 3. You examined Bender by lifting his T-shirt and asked one of the guards for a knife. You said that you needed to open up Bender in a certain place in order to help him because he was suffering from a pneumothorax. You were not given a knife, but about 30 minutes later Spaga allegedly came into the shed and said that an ambulance was on its way from Banja Luka. You are said to have massaged Bender all this time, dabbing him with a moist rag. You supposedly weeping the entire time. Bender supposedly told you why he had been hurt. He said that he needed help because he was dying. You told him you could not help him and he would be taken by ambulance to Banja Luka. He said he did not want to go to Banja Luka. And after that this, he showed no more signs of life. You supposedly tried to revive Bender with mouth-to-mouth resuscitation and cardiac massage but without success. Soon after, the lifeless Bender was carried out of the shed and put into the ambulance that had arrived. And you were asked if you could remember that incident. And what you told the German investigator was, according to the document I have in front of me: "This is a fairy tale. This did not happen. If it had happened, I would remember it. Somebody has dreamt this up to make himself seem important and turn me into a hero. But I do not need this." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, -- let me tell you. Either I'm a fool or someone who's not worthy to be walking around. Not even a person who is illiterate would do something like that. I apologise. You read it out. But I quite simply don't know what to say about that. It's such a -- it's so confused. These words are so confused. Only a schizophrenic could say something like that. I don't understand where this came from and I don't understand what it is. Believe me, sir. Believe me. That's the truth. I simply can't understand it. I don't understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. But don't put the blame necessarily on the interpreters, Mr. Ackerman. Dr. Sabanovic, look at me --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Your Honour, I think there's some confusion. He understands --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. But he's not answering the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, he is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The way he's answering it is obliquely. This is what we have to establish.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But Your Honour, it's been put to him and he's asking us if he remembers it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. And instead of answering that question, he's going to the substance. This is --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the difficulty is -- and I repeat. I am objecting to this line of questioning. What is the relevance of any of this to the case for Mr. Brdjanin? We're just going forever round in circles, it seems to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But let the Tribunal draw conclusions from that, if it is so, Ms. Korner. I mean, at the present moment I do understand that Mr. Ackerman has every right to test the witness, putting us in a position to be able to -- to decide how much weight to give to the evidence of this witness. This is what he is trying to do. And I'm not going to stop him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I understand that, Your Honour, and I'd almost given up objecting. But in fact that answer was a part of a statement that apparently the German police had that they put to him and he said that was a fairytale. Now, how does that assist Your Honours, may I ask in reaching a conclusion as to the weight of this witness's evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, it would all have depended on the way he would have answered the question. It could well be that there was a second question in the pipeline waiting after that, had he said "yes, I remember being asked that and I remember giving that answer."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Or Mr. Ackerman was expecting the kind of reply that he actually got. How do I know?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I think -- it's clear that Mr. Ackerman and I need to have -- raise matters before Your Honour. But I'll sit down at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I really would like the witness to look at page 20 of the B/C/S translation of his German statement, because I really don't think he understood what it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me -- let me explain again the question to him. Mr. Ackerman -- Dr. Sabanovic, look at me, please. Dr. Sabanovic, Mr. Ackerman read out to you from the statement that we have been given supposedly telling us what question the investigator put to you -- the German investigator put to you and what you had said. What we want to know is whether you remember being told this story by the investigator, telling you someone has told us that this and this and this happened, and that I don't answered, "This is a fairytale." Do you remember being questioned and do you remember answering, "This is a fairytale," this is pure imagination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is the first time I've heard this here. This is the first time I've heard this. I don't remember about -- anything about that. No one asked me that question. And this is the first time I have heard this, and I am surprised by this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So Mr. Ackerman, you've got your answer now. You may proceed with the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, in your statement to the Prosecutor, on page 3 at the bottom of the page, the last paragraph, you told the Prosecutor's Office, according to this translation, the following: "Two or three months before the takeover of Sanski Most, non-Serbs living in non-Serbian parts of town had begun guarding their areas because they were afraid. For example, in the settlement of Mahala." Is that the case? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the next page, it says that you said: "Armed Croat and Muslim civilians stood guard during the evening to ensure the safety of civilians living in those parts. All these factors led to Muslims and Croats organising the patrols, especially during the evening." That's also true, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you told us, sir, yesterday that you had seen Mr. Brdjanin at Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you told us you had seen him when he left the middle stable; correct?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were you?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in front -- I was in front. Outside. I then turned around to the -- towards the other stables. I was in the infirmary at the time, but I didn't go in at the time because a speech was being given and you didn't have the right to enter the stables.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were in the infirmary and he came out of stable 3 -- or the middle stable, which would be -- the middle stable.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Went from the infirmary, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's where you saw him and recognised him; correct?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in your statement to the Prosecutor, you told the Prosecutor -- it's page 14 of your statement -- that he was there on two occasions. Yesterday you said you were only sure about one of those. And when you told the Prosecutor about his visit, you said "It was toward the end of July 1992"; correct?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also told us that either a policeman or a nurse told you before the arrival that Brdjanin was coming. Can you tell us who told you that?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a policeman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you said police or a nurse. Now you know it's a policeman?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A policeman or a nurse. A nurse wears a uniform just like a policeman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you don't remember who it was.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's nothing for me to remember. I don't know the names of any of the policemen, neither the first nor the last name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you did know the names of the nurses.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Aco was one name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yeah. We talked about that person yesterday, didn't we?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You think that was the person who told you Brdjanin was coming?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And others, not just him. Several of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday at page 43 of the LiveNote you were talking about these visits. You talked about Brdjanin and Zupljanin and Kupresanin visiting the camp. And you referred to it as 3N, Manjaca 3N?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that meant the three people from the Banja Luka Crisis Staff. And their names all ended in N. That was your testimony; right?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like you now to be shown, sir, Exhibit DB87. Now, sir, on the 20th of February of 2001, an investigator from the Prosecutor's Office showed you a number of photographs and asked you if among those photographs you could see this Mr. Brdjanin who you knew well because you'd seen him on television and could recognise him from across the yard; right?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were given that opportunity, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I said that I didn't know who Brdjanin was when looking at these photographs. When I have a look at him now I still wouldn't know. I didn't give an affirmative answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, you could not pick Mr. Brdjanin out from these photographs that you were shown, could you? You were shown 12 photographs, and you couldn't identify Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I think if the case is that Mr. Brdjanin was never there, it ought to be put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I missed that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner -- Sorry, Mr. Ackerman. Ms. Korner is suggesting that if you contend that your client was never present in Manjaca, you should put it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I suggest to you that you did not see Mr. Brdjanin at Manjaca and that he was never there. And of course you will say to me, "You're wrong, Mr. Ackerman"; right?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I won't say that you're wrong, but that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, it's like distinction between the infirmary and the hospital. We stop --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We stop there. You've finished, Mr. Ackerman. Madam Fauveau, you have the option of starting now and stopping in 12 minutes' time, to resume after the break. Or we'll take the break now and you start your cross-examination immediately after the break. I leave it entirely up to you. What do you prefer?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I can start now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Then proceed. Dr. Sabanovic, you are now going to be cross-examined by Defence counsel for General Talic. Madam Fauveau. Cross-examined by Ms. Fauveau-Ivanovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, in 1992, you were the deputy of the municipal assembly in Sanski Most; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did the last session of the municipal assembly take place at which you attended?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't answer that. That was a long time ago. If you're referring to the year 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm referring to 1992.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I couldn't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The day before yesterday you said that before 1990 you were a member of the League of Communists.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct to say that you became a member of the League of Communists in order to be able to assume the post of the chief of the -- of the head of the clinic in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was already elected, and then two hours later I got my booklet saying that I was a member of the League of Communists. My secretary in the health centre later became the secretary of the committee. He was in that selection and got the booklet in two hours' time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke on the 3rd of June, and you said that the Serbs had the desire to create a new state without Croats and without Muslims. Isn't it true that the Serbs didn't want to create a new state but that they wanted to remain within Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could put it that way, to remain within Yugoslavia. Yes, to remain in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in fact, the Croats wanted a new, independent state; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the Muslims wanted a new, independent Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was a referendum about that, and we know that that was -- they voted for that at the referendum and they voted for an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke about Milosevic. That was also on the 3rd of June. And you said that he was President of Serbia and the commander of the army. Isn't it true that the commander of the army was the President of the Presidency of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in April 1992, it was the Croat, Stipo Mesic.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Stipe Mesic was the commander of the Yugoslavia army and not Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not then. Later. The President of Serbia and then the President of Yugoslavia, which was formed by Serbian Montenegro. It was then that he was the commander of the armed forces of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. That's what I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But that was later. It wasn't in April 1992.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, for sure. But I don't know about that. There was some confusion about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said on the 3rd of June that your wife was a Serbian. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you have three sons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And all your sons have Muslim names. Their first names are Muslim first names; is that true?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The eldest one is Ernes. The second is Alen, and the third is Oliver.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you spoke about the certificates that you issued to persons who did not want to go to the army. And yesterday you said that these certificates weren't false. Do you have in front of you the statement that you gave to the Prosecutor in the year 2000? Do you have this statement?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it should probably be here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 3 of this statement -- I think it's also page 3 in the Serbo-Croat version. It's also page 3 in the Serbo-Croat version. The second paragraph, the third sentence in the second paragraph. In the English version it's also the second paragraph, the third sentence. You said: [In English]: "Most of the certificates I issued were false." [Interpretation] And today could you say whether these certificates were false or whether they weren't false?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a single certificate was false. Each certificate was issued to people who felt that they couldn't go to war and couldn't join in a war between two states -- couldn't join the fight between Croatia and Serbia. They didn't want to go. And that is either psychological or organic factor. People were perhaps ill and these people were of various -- of all nationalities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that case, why did you say in this written statement that most of these certificates were false?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, in people's case histories, people would give this information. They would always say that they were ill. And when we'd have a look, perhaps they could have gone in a war situation. But in that country, there was no war situation so I had to listen to the people and write down what they said and what I determined through laboratory examinations and other sorts of examinations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you spoke with the representative of the OTP, why did you say that these certificates or most of these certificates were false?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. The word "false," I don't know if I used that word. These certificates were given to people so that they wouldn't have to go and join a fight between other states. And Bosnia and Herzegovina was already an independent state and it had been recognised such by the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The war in Croatia did take place in 1991; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1991, I don't know. Around the beginning of 1991, 1992. Around those dates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in 1991, the army which was in Croatia, as well as in Bosnia, it was the JNA.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But the army which was fighting against Croatia, it wasn't the JNA. It wasn't only the JNA. It was the JNA which had gone to Serbia and elsewhere, but it wasn't in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Bosnia in 1991 was still part of Yugoslavia, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was at the beginning, and later -- it's all been written down. It's well known when -- it's a well-known fact when there was a referendum and when it became independent and was recognised by the United Nations. What I gave at the time, that took place at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know that you don't like dates very much. But if I say that Bosnia became independent on the 6th of April, 1992, could you accept that?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you accept that on the 6th of April, 1992 there was no more war in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. I don't know. In November 1992 I passed through Gradiska, and it's not possible to say that there was no war there, because part of Croatia had been occupied by Serbia, and there were UN troops and there was a zone where it hadn't been finished.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in any case, in any event, the JNA was no longer there.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps not.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would it be a good time to have a break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. We'll have a break of 15 minutes, resuming at 4.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I recognise Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, after returning from my spot over there, my colleagues here told me that the translations that were being done during the cross-examination of this witness were absolutely flawless, they were being done perfectly. And so I just want to publicly apologise to the translators if I criticised them -- and I did, I think -- that it was not the translation that was causing the problems that were happening this morning. And so to the extent that I can, I apologise to them publicly for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand from Madam Fauveau that she's going to take the rest of this day and maybe tomorrow with this witness. We have a witness here who's being -- who's waiting to testify, on the basis of indications I was given yesterday. The other matter I should mention straight away is although we managed to stop one of the witnesses, we have a witness here waiting to testify. I want to know perhaps what Your Honours think about the fact that if he doesn't start till Friday, he probably won't finish and we then have the week's break. I raise that now. I'm not going to stop that because I'm anxious to get the doctor away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you for raising the matter. Shall we postpone it until the very end of today's sitting, or do you need to know before that?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. I don't need -- I mean, both witnesses are here already. I don't need to know now. I'm merely pointing this out. But Your Honours may feel that it would be desirable if the doctor were able to leave at least tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll do our utmost. And if -- I don't know, Madam Fauveau, obviously I'm not going interfere with your cross-examination. But if it is at all possible to conclude today, you will try and conclude today.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will do my best. I will do my utmost to finish today. But it is quite possible that perhaps I will need another half an hour or very little for my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Fauveau. Please proceed. And Dr. Sabanovic, try to answer yes or no when that is possible, without going into details, because the more details you enter into, the longer you will stay here. Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you speak about certificates that you issued to persons who had been called up, you spoke about that and you said that some JNA officers came to see you. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these officers were polite talking to you?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They did not threaten you?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The day before yesterday - and it is the page 13 of the LiveNote - you said that these officers did not tell you that you did not have the right to issue the certificates.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you look at page 3 of your statement, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The statement to the OTP of 2000, 2001.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Towards the end of the second paragraph, you said: [In English] "At the time they were not unpleasant but they told me that I had no right to issue the permits any longer." [Interpretation] Well, why did you say this if you didn't think it true?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't perhaps consider it important, because there was no conflict between us, there were no words between us. So perhaps I just disregarded it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you spoke also about a colleague of yours, Bosko Grubisa by name. And you said that he was wearing a uniform.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you see him in the uniform for the first time?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was somewhere on the 25th or the 26th of April, when I was dismissed, when I was removed from my post of the head of the general specialist department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this Bosko Grubisa worked for the same health centre as you?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. An intern. Yes, he worked with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And since when did he work for that centre?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe he was there from 1992, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about 1991, 1992? Was he still working for the centre?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He wasn't on the front in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your written statement - and it is page 3. It is the statement to the OTP, page 3 in the English version, the very first sentence. And in the B/C/S version, it is the first paragraph and -- the first whole paragraph, the first sentence of it. You said that you already in July or August 1991 you felt tensions and the JNA, or more specifically the 6th Krajina Brigade had arrived into the area. Did you mean by this that the 6th Brigade arrived in the area of Sanski Most in July or August 1991?
