utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. It arrived sometime in the early days of March, the beginning of March 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the registrar please show P608, please, Exhibit P608.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it the order of the command of the 5th Corps?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't really know which corps, to be quite honest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doesn't it say at the top of the page to the left "The command of the 5th Corps"?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's right. But I don't know. I -- at that time I did know about the 5th Corps. I only know about the 5th Corps after 1992, in the course of the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the date on this order is the 1st of April, 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you look at the first paragraph immediately after number 1, below the words "I hereby issue this order." This is an order to the 6th Brigade to come to the area of Sanski Most; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we agree that the 6th Brigade received an order to deploy its forces in the area of Sanski Most on the 1st of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. Possibly. I did not follow that, and as to the dates, no, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The question before the current one, the witness said, "Da, da," but it didn't get interpreted and the answer says "no interpretation," but he did answer it yes, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's clarify that. Dr. Sabanovic, immediately prior to the last question you were asked, you were asked the following question: "If you look at the first paragraph immediately after number 1, below the words "I hereby issue this order." This is an order to the 6th Brigade to come to the area of Sanski Most; is that correct?" What was your answer? Because the interpreters didn't get it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't know what you answered or -- what was your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know when it came. I know that the 6th Krajina Brigade arrived sometime in April to Sanski Most and that they communicated with Colonel Basara and had some talks with them and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the registrar please show P609.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't this the report of the command of the 5th Corps dated the 2nd of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And passage 2, paragraph 2, the paragraph which comes after "2," it speaks about the deployment of the 6th Brigade in the area of Sanski Most; would that be true?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And according to this report, the brigade should be deployed in the area in Sanski Most until the 3rd of April, 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 3rd of June, you spoke about the checkpoints which were set up by the Serbs, and you said that before the brigade came there were no such checkpoints. Could you be more precise and tell us when were the Serb checkpoints set up in the area of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot be quite precise, because it was at that chief period before the war. Perhaps it could have been March, April, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you look at your statement which you gave to the OTP, page 3 of the English version, the last passage. And in B/C/S version, it is the first passage on page 4. And it is in the middle of the paragraph. You said that the Serbs set up their checkpoints after the 19th of May, 1992. It's page 4, the first passage.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. This is a mistake. One shouldn't -- that was earlier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then why did you say that it was after the 19th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I fail to understand this, I must say. In April, yes. But now you say May. In April, that is possible. But in May -- in May, by that time everything was already organised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the statement that you have before you, is it your statement?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, whose could it be? If it's here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you had the opportunity to go through the statement before you came to testify here.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't paying attention and I never gave any thoughts to dates. A month here, a month there. You knew what was happening. But I'm not a military person to keep up with those statistics. So perhaps it was a mistake not to do that. But I never gave it a thought, and it was a long time ago, and so ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I do not know whether the witness still has before him P608.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wouldn't think so. It's not normal that the registry leaves the documents lying on the table there during the break, I suppose. 608.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is paragraph 2 of item 1. That is, this is a passage -- paragraph which doesn't give with a number. Is it correct that the command of the 5th Corps ordered, among other things, the -- to prevent inter-ethnic conflicts and the establishment, the setting up of roadblocks?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is how it was stated by the 6th Krajina Brigade, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please now look at 609. The version in English is page 2, and B/C/S page 3. It is the paragraph which begins with number "3," "I have decided." In this report -- in this paragraph it is also indicated that General Talic decided to prevent the establishment of the road -- the setting up of the roadblocks; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this -- and General Talic signed this document, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you spoke -- no, it was the day before yesterday, on the 3rd of June, page 14 of the LiveNote. You spoke about the guards which were organised by non-Serbs in order to protect their villages. Could you tell us when did the non-Serbs organise those guards.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, before these hard times started -- once again, I can't give you the date. Hard times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the non-Serbs also set up their checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not checkpoints. They had village guards, and the Serbs had their checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could one say that these non-Serb guards were established two or three months before Sanski Most was taken by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'd say so. But it's very difficult for me to speak about any dates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, one can say that the non-Serbs organised their guards before the Serbs set up their checkpoints; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The checkpoints were already in existence. It was the checkpoints which conduced to the village guards organised by Croats and Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct to say that the non-Serbs organised those guards in the town of Sanski Most as well? That is, in those parts of -- in the part of the town where they were the majority.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those Muslims and Croats organised those guards. They were armed, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why, yes, surely. No dilemma.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there were such guards in Mahala too, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, there were armed individuals in Mahala, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The day before yesterday, page 18, you spoke about the attack on the municipal hall building in Sanski Most. Did you see that attack?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any military, any troop movements during that attack?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you do not know who took part in that attack, do you?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police took part, all the police. And the police had already been split. There was the Serb police, and they participated in it; all the armed ones who sided with the Chetniks, that is, the Serb police and the others. Well, the Serb authorities by and large.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there was an exchange of fire between the Serbian police and the Muslim and Croat police; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were in the municipality for a very short time. Then they left the municipality and went towards a village called Poljak. So they came to an end quite rapidly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At a certain point in time -- on the 3rd of June, page 18 of the LiveNote, you said that they were all members of the military. When you say that they were all soldiers, do you mean to say that everyone wearing a uniform was a soldier?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everyone wearing a uniform and carrying weapons. That's what it was called at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 4 of your statement. It's the second paragraph in the English version on page 4, and it's page 4 in the second paragraph in the Serb-Croat version. You said that you had seen Serb children with weapons. How old were these children?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were young people, 17 or 18 years old.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were arrested on the 26th of May, 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said on the 3rd of June - it's page 21 of the LiveNote - you said that your papers, your personal paper, had been burnt.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us who burnt your papers.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people who escorted me from the hospital to my home. I said that yesterday. The people who took me from the hospital to my home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did they burn your identity papers?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In front of the house. At the stop where we stopped in front of the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, when you had returned from the hospital and returned home, how many policemen got out of the vehicle?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Four. One came out with me immediately to talk to me, but there were four sitting in the vehicle and they came out later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So all four men came out of the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Later on they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 3rd of June, at page 20 you said: [In English] "Only one of them got out of the van."

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning, I was escorted to the house -- to the fence in front of the house and then escorted me into the house. And then the other three got out of the vehicle too. So the other three were outside too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You spoke about - and it's still on the 3rd of June - about a Catholic person who was detained in the Hasan Kikic hall. He was detained with you there. And he had been wounded in the shelling.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that this shelling had been carried out by the 6th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were not personally present when this shelling took place.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because I was already imprisoned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't have any personal knowledge of the identity of the perpetrator of the shelling.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 6th Krajina Brigade was deployed between Sanski Most -- above Sanski Most, above Mahala, about 3 kilometres away on a hill called Magarice, and the artillery was there. That's a hundred per cent sure. I knew about that. I saw them. And I was in contact with Colonel Basara and with officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the 26th of May, was there any shelling of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you personally, you didn't see the shelling.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't possible for me to see it because I had been imprisoned. I was imprisoned after the 26th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you spoke about the destruction of the roof of your house.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was this roof destroyed?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Immediately after I had left. As soon as I had left, that took place. There was zoljas fired at the house. They fired at the house. The roof was destroyed, the door, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you -- when the roof of your house was destroyed, at that time you were already in prison.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd already left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you didn't see it being destroyed.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you said that a young Muslim and a young Serb put the fire out in your house. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't set fire to it. No, they put it out. Yes, that's right. Yes, a Muslim and a Serb, two boys who lived in the neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This Serb, was he a soldier?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The day before yesterday you spoke about your arrival in the Manjaca camp, and you said that you had seen the murder of two persons. It's in the LiveNote, page 51. It was a young man, Mehardzic and a dentist called Biscevic.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you have a look at your written statement, it's page -- it's on page 7. It's the paragraph before the last one in the English version. And in the Croatian version, it's page 8, the first paragraph on page 8. You spoke about the death of this young person called Mehardzic. But then you say: [In English] "From my position, I was not able to witness the other murders."

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You didn't mention the murder of the dentist called Biscevic.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps I didn't. I saw a third person too, but I didn't sit down and think about what was being done. It was all done very quickly. But there was another person I saw who served in the army, in the JNA before the war in the time of the real Yugoslavia. I saw him in Manjaca, and he also died. That's for sure. That's a hundred per cent certain. His name is Hadziahmetovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if I am following your testimony correctly, in your statement given in the year 2000, 2001 you saw one murder. On the 3rd of June, you saw two. And today you're saying that you witnessed three; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You should have done that immediately after that, and then we would be speaking in different terms. For me to be think about this ten years after the event and for me to refer to everything -- well, I apologise to you. You're behaving in a very correct manner. But perhaps there are certain discrepancies here, given the amount of time that has passed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you would allow for the possibility that there is certain information that isn't correct in your statements.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how to formulate this. Mistakes -- perhaps it's a matter of forgetting something and as a result not everything was -- was stated. There's no other way for me to interpret this and now that I have these things before me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 3rd of June - it's page 47 of the LiveNote - you said that the persons who were detained in Manjaca and who came from Sanski Most and Kljuc weren't soldiers.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Yes. I said yes. But they weren't soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on this occasion you said that there was no war and no resistance had been mounted in the city.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was no resistance on our part. That was an aggression, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you explained -- in another statement that you gave you explained why you said at a certain point in time that it was war?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And yesterday you said -- you said that you had said that because: [In English] [Previous translation continues] ... "It was called war." [Interpretation] When you say that it was called war --

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never mentioned that. I said that there were -- the military police was there because it was war and that was on the Serbian side, or rather, the side that was against us. The Croats and the Muslims didn't mount any resistance, so you could say that there was no war, given that there was only one side. If there is to be a war, you need two sides. That's what I said yesterday, and I'll repeat that again today. Not a single Serb in Sanski Most was wounded, let alone killed. Not even wounded. There was no shooting from our side. We were rounded up and taken away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree that a state of war hadn't been declared in the Sanski Most area in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't think it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the registrar show the witness Prosecutor's Exhibit P642.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this a report from the 1st Krajina Corps command?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the date is the 27th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 27th of May, 1992. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you have a look at the end of the first paragraph. It's on page 1. It's just above number "2." It starts with the words "at about 15 hours."

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can see that. That's not correct. There were no Green Berets in Sanski Most. Throughout the entire period of the war, they were never there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Allow me to ask you the question.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This paragraph describes an incident in the Sanski Most area; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And according to this report, the Green Berets attacked a convoy. Could you answer the question. Because I don't think it was interpreted.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no Green Berets, and there couldn't have been an attack. They didn't exist.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the registrar show the witness Exhibit P659.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this a report from the 1st Krajina Corps command dated the 3rd of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you have a look again at the -- towards the end of paragraph 1, just before number "2," it says that there are still individuals and groups -- extremist individuals and groups acting in the Prijedor, Sanski Most, and Kljuc areas; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says here, but that's not correct. In Sanski Most. I don't know about the other two places, Prijedor and Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's something in the Serbo-Croat version which wasn't translated into English. I'm going to read it in Serbo-Croat so that the interpreters can read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "It is to be expected that there will be further fighting in the entire area of the zone of responsibility and that there will be new focal points."

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no -- there was no fighting in Sanski Most, and there were no focal points, no places where there were hot points.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. It's quite right. It hasn't been translated. But I don't think it said -- if the translation that's come up is right, it's the area of the zone of responsibility, which as I understand it covers the whole of the first 1st KK, not just Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you are right, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can I while I'm on my feet just make the point that we can all read what's in the documents, but whether we're achieving much by asking the witness whether he agrees with it or not is another matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, it -- you would have certainly noticed, Ms. Korner, that throughout the last two, three weeks it has -- one of the points that has strongly been contested by the two Defence teams is what exactly happened in Sanski Most before the -- the day or up to the day or on the day when the municipal buildings and the police -- so this is something which is very hotly contested by -- by the Defence, and they are trying to question each witness that we have had, starting with Judge Draganovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. We're having -- well, there are two issues, Your Honour. One is, as I understand it, although no positive suggestion has been made about who it was who was supposed to be there, who was doing the fighting. All that's been suggested along the lines of what was put to Judge Draganovic was that he was saying there was no resistance in order to get his --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, no. Oh, no. Oh, no. The contestation --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I don't want to waste time because I want the witness to finish. All I'm saying is that by simply reading documents to him which say what the 1st KK documents say, which he hasn't seen, and the question that's being asked is, "Do you see that's what it says, and he says, "Yes, but I don't agree with it."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, you have done exactly the same thing with several witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that everything that is written in this report is not true, and you also say that there was no resistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He didn't --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as Sanski Most is concerned. I don't know about other places other than Sanski Most. There was no resistance in Sanski Most, and there was no shooting. That's -- that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nevertheless there were armed Croats and Muslims in Sanski Most itself.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Weapons were surrendered when it started in May. In the camp I saw them bringing it in. In Betonirka they'd bring it in by tractor or in carts drawn by horses. These were hunting guns, et cetera, so I'm sure that there was no resistance, and I'm convinced of this. I know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you in Betonirka -- when you were in Betonirka, it was from the 27th or 28th of May; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, around the 28th of May. Because on the 26th I was in the toilet -- I was locked up in the toilet in MUP, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the fighting in Sanski Most was on the 27th of May; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, around the 27th or 28th, something like that. There was no fighting though. People were brought in and halls were filled up, but there was no fighting. I didn't hear any shooting, apart from shells that would be fired at surrounding villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I invite you to move to something different now, Madam Fauveau, please. I think you've made your point and he's made his point on this particular topic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were in Manjaca, in the Manjaca camp, you were on good terms with Command Popovic; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the -- after June. Up until June, it was necessary to resist this psychologically. But as time passed, people became convinced that I wasn't the person that they had been told I was according to information from Sanski Most, and this was proved later on and I was released and they greeted me correctly when we parted ways.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned seven persons who had apparently been thrown into the Vrbas River. When did this happen?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I heard. Well, it happened when a large group arrived from Sanski Most towards the end of July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You heard about this but you didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about it, but I didn't see it. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You couldn't confirm that the person who told you that was telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I couldn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke about death certificates that Colonel Popovic asked you to write and which didn't contain the exact cause of death. Isn't it true to say that Colonel Popovic then sent these certificates, these death certificates, with -- which mentioned a false cause of death to his superiors?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what he did with them. But as they are nowhere among these documents from the 1st Krajina Corps and the Crisis Staff, well, that's why it surprises me. But as Mr. Popovic isn't here to give his opinion and his testimony, et cetera -- we parted ways in a nice way. I don't know where he is and I haven't heard anything about him. I'm in Banja Luka very often now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Colonel Popovic tell you why he needed false certificates?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't say anything about that. We didn't talk -- there was not much conversation. Why? Because people were killed. So that it didn't seem as if they died in Manjaca. Probably for that reason.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you allow for the possibility that these false certificates were sent by Colonel Popovic to his superiors.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what he did. It wasn't for me to think about that. I wasn't an active officer. I wasn't a soldier in Manjaca. And I had no authority to deal with this.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the registrar show the witness Exhibit DT2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this an order from the command of the 1st Krajina Corps dated the 7th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you have a look at paragraph 2. It was ordered that the prisoners should be allowed to receive cigarettes and food from their families, from the Red Cross, and from other religious and humanitarian organisations.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it true to say that Merhamet went to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They say that they went there. But believe me, I wasn't in contact with Merhamet and I didn't see what they brought with them. They did come, but I had no contact with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you don't deny the fact that Merhamet went to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't deny that. I didn't have any contact with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And according to paragraph 3 of this order, it was necessary to behave towards the prisoners in a humane and dignified manner, without violence, insults, and it was necessary to provide them with accommodation, sustenance, and medical care for the sick in accordance with the provisions of international war law. That's what it says in this order; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says. And it's written very nicely. But that's not what actually happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Colonel Popovic didn't respect this order.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It was not like that, and I do not know who it was that did not respect it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe you were in the same stable as Omer Filipovic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Judge Draganovic was also in that stable, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said sometime ago that the night when Omer Filipovic was killed, you were sleeping in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 3rd June, on page 68, you said the last time that Omer Filipovic left the stable he could not walk under his own steam, that he had to be carried.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the night when Omer Filipovic left the stable for the last time, were you still in the stable?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And therefore the statement, according to which Omer Filipovic that last night left the stable running, would not be true, would it?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He couldn't. No way. After the few days which preceded it, he simply couldn't do it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is in the testimony of witness 7.77, page 5089 of the French transcript of the 26th of April. You also spoke about a representative of the Red Cross. Did you personally have the opportunity to talk with the Red Cross representatives -- or representative?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, only when they come to the infirmary. And then we talk about medicines they need to bring. I didn't really dare, because I'd been advised not to talk with them too much, so I didn't just for the sake of my safety.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you confirm that other prisoners had the opportunity to talk with the representative of the Red Cross without the presence of the guards?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, it did happen. But after that major problems ensued, because night falls and evil comes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you said that in Manjaca you were hit by only one person.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was right -- that was immediately after my arrival. That was only that first day in the evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 3rd June, on page 67 of the transcript, you said: [In English] "Nobody beat me."

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't count that, because that was sort of putting on record. He didn't beat me as we were getting off the truck. But only when we were down there. And I explained that. When we arrived in the stable and I was talking with military persons, when that one Bula made a sign of cross over me, that policeman when he -- but what I said. That I would never be able to learn, they wouldn't learn it by the morning and I wouldn't want to. Then he hit me and then I flew about 2 metres over all the others. I already explained that. But nobody beat me, and I do not call this beating properly and I wasn't beaten there after that ever. It was only on that first day, and I never said that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said on page 57 of the 3rd of June: [In English] That there were 8.700 prisoners in Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were over 8.000. That was the largest number. But it varied. There would be several hundred -- or several thousand -- there was never an equal number of prisoners for two days running.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I tell you that there were 5.300-something, would you be able to go along with that figure?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that figure also held true on some days. Sometimes even less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I tell you that according to this statement, the number 5.436 is the total number of prisoners who went through Manjaca. Would you go along with that statement?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. As far as they explained to me. I couldn't count them, because I couldn't do that. But in the commander usually said how many of them were, that is how busy I would be kept, how many people I had to examine and so on and so forth. And this figure did come up of over 8.000, and it was mentioned by people who were running the place. I can't call them administrators because it's a civilian word.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you spoke about Enver Burnic. And you said -- and that is on page 9 of the LiveNote that Enver Burnic frequently came to Manjaca with the police and also went away with them. I'd like to have this clarified. Do you mean -- did you mean that Burnic worked for the police?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was kept in Sana. He was under police custody, but he came with them several times in Manjaca. When the policemen came from Sanski Most for investigation, he came with them several times and he came the last time when I told you that they suffocated in the truck because of the lack of air and emaciation and so on and so forth. Then he and that other one, that dentistry student returned that last time with that group. Those -- those who drove away, those who had suffocated, those who had suffocated. After that he never came again nor really was he seen again. And every trace of him is lost. I mean, we do not know what happened to him, just as we do not know what happened that those who had suffocated. I'm certain about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why did Burnic come and leave with the police?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke about a guard called Bula. Can you tell us until when was this guard in Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the very end. Until I left. I said yesterday I don't really hold it much against the police. Whenever we were lined up, whenever there was some trouble, there were always those who ran the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it true that after Filipovic's death some guards were removed?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that. To be quite honest, yes, they changed. Some left, some came. But there were also some who were there throughout.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were released in November 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement you said that you were released on the 24th of November. This is page 17.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Weren't you set free on the 14th of November in point of fact?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are two things in collision. I could never really accept either, because I didn't know the date of my release and I never gave it a thought afterwards. I do not deny it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you were released, there were also other people who were set free; isn't it true?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there were also exchanges of prisoners, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you spoke about some Chetniks who were outside the camp. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. But these are Chetniks who were brought to me. I examined them. And they went on a hunger strike, and they were under custody. And after that, I was asked a few days later what to do with them and I said they should be sent to a military hospital in order to avoid endocrinological changes in their organisms. That is a sickness. And they were driven away and I don't know what happened after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it true that at the time when you were in Manjaca outside the camp there was a great deal of insecurity because of the extremist groups which were out of control?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. Possibly. It was said that there was security to avoid their breaking in. Nobody was allowed to enter the camp. Even though those who came to supply the camp, when the police from Sanski Most, Prijedor, or Kljuc came, that is where they usually came from -- we knew when they were call -- when there were roll calls then. But it didn't happen very often. And they did on such occasions at times come in and beat, but it didn't happen much. Seldom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it true that the Manjaca detainees at that time in 1992 could not be released without having some accommodations provided for them elsewhere, precisely because of these extremist groups?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were -- no, not near. They were usually taken to Banja Luka for exchange or to Travnik, to Jajce, to Knin, and those are those for the most part. They went to Banja Luka or went back to the places where they had come from. But that was a smaller number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you spoke about a visit how General Talic visited the camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... put the question, since you're opening something different after the break. We'll break for 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau. Wait, wait, wait, wait. We've still got to wait for the accused.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you spoke about the visit which General Talic made to the Manjaca camp. Did you personally see General Talic there?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far were you from General Talic or the person that you saw?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 30 to 40 metres, give or take.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you knew General Talic -- that you had known General Talic before the war.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. Before the war, I'd ask if General Talic knew Colonel Muharem Talic who came to be his assistant and who was from the same place as I was. That is how I knew him. On the 29th and 30th, he was in Sanski Most and then he returned. When they saw the situation, then he was returned from Banja Luka to Belgrade two days later. But I knew Mr. General during the war and before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me. But what was on the 29th and 30th? Who was it on the 29th and 30th in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The then-General Talic's assistant. And he has the same last name, Muharem Talic. Colonel Muharem Talic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yeah, right. But can you tell me where did you meet General Talic? How do you know him?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know him from television and like this, by sight, from Banja Luka. There were no official meetings or something. I know General Talic by sight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that -- when did General Talic become the [Realtime transcript read in error "member"] commander of the 5th Corps?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I heard that he became the commander of the 5th Corps towards the very end of the war -- towards the beginning of the war, on the eve of the war. But don't ask me where.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I'm going to interrupt about the translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... it was when did General Talic become the commander of the 5th Corps. And it's been translated as a member.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you are right, Ms. Korner. The -- you are absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think obviously the translation into B/C/S was all right. But in English, it was wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that it was well interpreted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you ask the witness when did General Talic become the commander of the 5th Corps? That's what we were told. In English at least.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But the interpretation into B/C/S was correct, and because the witness answered that General Talic became the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. If Your Honour looks at the question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I know. You are right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're a hundred per cent right. But for the record, you did understand that the question was related to when General Momir Talic became commander, when you came to know that General Talic became commander of the 5th Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness nods.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because we have to -- the computer doesn't tell me --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know when did General Talic come to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. These are military matters. I did not follow that. I wasn't interested in such things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But when did you have the occasion to see General Talic in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Banja Luka -- what do I know. It was on the eve of the war. I went to Banja Luka. I had now -- I never came across any problems when going to Banja Luka and other places. And on television.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who was General Talic's Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. I know that my neighbour came. That is what he told us in Sanski Most that, he had been sent to be General Talic's assistant both the name sake, same surname. He came to Sanski Most on the 29th. He came to the camp, visited the camp, returned and then two or three days later he went to Belgrade, so that his village went unscathed until 1995, when Arkan returned to his village. His village Sehovci was quiet until 1995. That was the colonel's birthplace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This person, Muharem --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please answer the question and nothing but the question. The question was a very simple one. Do you know who was General Talic's Chief of Staff? You either know or you don't know. If you know, you tell us. Well, that's it, why do I have to hear all this story. I mean, this will keep you here until tomorrow if you continue like this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I won't. Thank you very much. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This person, Muharem Talic, your neighbour, he is a Muslim, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was a member of the Serb army, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Yugoslav People's Army. That is where he became a colonel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you said on page 39 that General Talic had visited the camp on two occasions. Do you remember that? It was yesterday.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember it, and I quote. He was 30 or 40 metres away from me. He was in the command. I never said that he was in the stables. And as I heard from the police, he came to visit the troops that were in the training ground at Manjaca, because Manjaca is a training centre. And he was in the command then, and I saw him as he was coming out, when he was on his way, and that is sure. And others also told me that he would be coming. He did not give any lectures. He did not visit the stables.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you said that he came twice.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you look at your written statement, the statement to the OTP, page 15 in the English version. It is the second -- the third paragraph, the last sentence. In the B/C/S, it is the penultimate paragraph, the last sentence. You said: [In English] "As far as I know, this was Talic's only visit."

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is -- I stand by this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You stand by one visit or two visits?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him twice. Twice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if I tell you that you are wrong and that it was not General Talic, would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you telling us that General Talic came to the camp because you had seen him or because somebody had told you that?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I had seen him. That is why I said that. That is why I say that. And I also heard in advance that he would be coming.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that person whom you saw, you would not say that it is possible that it was somebody else?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't far away, so I cannot say that it was not he. True, there are people who look alike, but I do not think that that was so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you are not really sure that it was General Talic nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I am sure, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke about the conditions in Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the registrar show the witness Exhibit P807.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you have a look at photograph number 8, the one which is mistakenly marked as a clinic, as an infirmary. This photograph represents a place where you were able to place your patients.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it correct to say that the infirmary was elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We call it a clinic. It was at a different place, outside the fence. This is inside the camp, behind the first stables.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in fact in the Manjaca camp, there were two places where you could treat sick people; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you have a look at Exhibit P808 now. Is this a photograph of inmates in Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And all the detainees, all the inmates in this photograph, have a blanket underneath them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Here it's correct. These are more serious cases, et cetera. Yes, that's true. You can see there are two men who have plaster casts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the men who have their -- who have plaster casts, they were given treatment.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And behind the beds of these persons, you can see canisters with water; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't really see water canisters. In front of the heads? Yes, I can see two canisters, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, there are several of them but some are concealed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can see two. Maybe a third one towards the end, but I'm not sure. I can see two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The day before yesterday you spoke about the examination of four persons who had a skin disease.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the very first day, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the hearing here -- it's page 55 of the LiveNote, dated the 3rd of June -- you said that the soldiers brought medical supplies a few days later.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then with these medical supplies, were you able to treat the sick people with these medical supplies?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the police delivered these medical supplies, did you have any medical supplies?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that case, why did you say in your written statement given to the Office of the Prosecutor - and it's on page 8 in the English version and it's page 8 in the Serbo-Croat version. It's the last sentence in the second paragraph in the English version. And it's the last sentence in the penultimate paragraph in the Serbo-Croat version. You said: [In English] "I was not permitted to treat them." [Interpretation] Didn't you say that?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I suppose it's a translation error again. Do you admit that this might be possible?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what it is, but I never said that. That's the first time I examined people in Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the truth is that in fact the soldiers brought medicine and you were able to treat these people.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also examined a young man whose shoulder had been dislocated.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you recommended that he be taken to Banja Luka; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in fact -- and in fact he was taken to the hospital in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And later on you received news about this young man.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, later, when I had left and gone to Switzerland. From Karlovac this person contacted me over the phone, this young man. He said he was well and he thanked me for what I had done and he thanked those who had helped him in the hospital in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in fact this young man was taken to the Banja Luka hospital and he was treated there; is that true?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to read an extract from a report from an international organisation written on the basis of a Merhamet report with regard to Manjaca, about Manjaca. It's a report dated June 1992. It's Exhibit P763, communicated -- disclosed to us pursuant to Rule 70 [As interpreted]. It's page 3, and it's the first paragraph. [In English] "A delegation from --"

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's come up at Rule 60. It should read Rule 70.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: 70, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "A delegation from Merhamet visited a prisoner camp at Manjaca mountain where 1.200 persons are held by the army. Material conditions were poor, especially concerning hygiene. But there were no signs of maltreatment or execution of prisoners."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you answer, Dr. Sabanovic, Ms. Korner --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I wasn't asked, Your Honour, but I'm happy for it to be dealt with in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I've been asked on an earlier occasion with another witness. So I'm happy --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is what I wanted to ensure, because this is also being extracted from a confidential document.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I apologise. I'll do it next time. But as I asked this to -- with regard to the preceding witness, I thought that this authorisation was still valid. Next time I will ask for permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's what should be done on a regular basis. Don't think anything for granted because each time the question may turn out to be different and one answer could lead to another question and so on and so forth. So we have to be extremely careful. Thank you. You may answer the question. Doctor, the question is: "A delegation from Merhamet visited a prisoner camp at Manjaca mountain where 1.200 persons are held by the army. Material conditions were poor, especially concerning hygiene. But there were no signs of maltreatment or execution of prisoners." Now, your question, Madam Fauveau, to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you agree with this report?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw them in Manjaca, nor did they have a look at the hygienic conditions or anything else. I'm not aware of this. I'm not aware of them being there and contacting me, and they didn't check on the hygienic conditions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. But again, I mean, you're not answering the question, doctor. The question was: Would you -- if assuming for a moment -- accept for a moment that what is contained in this report, namely that Merhamet reported on what they found in Manjaca and that they stated the words -- or made the statement that I told you, that I read out to you, would you agree that they gave a faithful description of what there was in Manjaca; yes or no? It's not a question of whether they went --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. That's your answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Prosecutor showed you a video cassette of the Manjaca camp. I'm going to ask you to have a look at the following part of the same video, an extract which contains Paddy Ashdown's statement when he left the Manjaca camp. And I'm going to ask you to read the subtitles in Serbo-Croat because the sound is very bad.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the video be shown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This time it will be your turn to tell the technicians when to stop.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that I've explained everything very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To them already.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I think that they know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. In other words we cannot depend on the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the video be shown.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, can you read the phrase which is on your screen.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Can you read it out so that the interpreters will translate it to us, because we don't know your language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "When leaving, he stated that however dismal things might appear".

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you show the following sequence.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Further on. Further on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you read that now, please.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "It seems that this camp is being run correctly."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, this video dates back to August 1992. And do you agree with this statement?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, let's say yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I apologise. I've finished earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Okay. Thank you, Madam Fauveau. I suppose the other witness has already been --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Taken away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- Taken away.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I think just on the basis of that last one. Re-examined by Ms. Korner:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Sabanovic, you were asked having seen in fact not what the commentators said, do you agree with the statement that the camp is being run correctly? And you said yes, you did agree with that statement.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't answer with yes or no here.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. My question was precise. In August 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. The people who seemed to be in a good condition towards the end. Well that's what they said because they had to say such things. That's why I said yes, that was a reason. I could change many things here at this trial, but I'll mention this later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If on the basis of the war I'm told about the doors and where the doors are and then you try to judge whether someone is guilty or not, well, some people might know better than I do what's correct and what isn't. Then that surprises me a bit, so I have to react in this way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. I think the question that you were asked was did you agree with the statement that the camp was being run correctly. And you said --

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- that you couldn't -- you said yes. First of all, do you agree from what you've described to us that this camp was being run correctly, properly?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He has just answered that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I know he has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He answered it with reference to a particular point in time, Madam Fauveau. That's August of 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat that answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear what you said. I heard you said Kranja [phoen] or something like that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that this had all been edited, set up. If I were here -- if I stayed here for a month, we wouldn't be able to arrive at the truth, because all these documents, et cetera, they have -- they contain many things which unfortunately couldn't be explained that easily. So sometimes I skip over something, and I regret that such things happened. It's difficult for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Sabanovic, all I want you to just concentrate on is this: You have described to us what you say happened in the camp, the beatings and everything like that. Is what you have told us about that the truth?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More than the truth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right at the beginning you looked at the list of the Geneva Conventions that was sent to the camp. You were asked by me whether or not those conventions had been obeyed by the people who ran the camp. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you again. Were the conditions that are set out in that sheet of paper followed by the guards, the commanders of the camp?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The Geneva Conventions weren't respected, not in any sense.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Dr. Sabanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Dr. Sabanovic, we have come to the end of your testimony. You will not be asked any further questions now, and you will be able to return to your country and to your work. But before you leave this courtroom, may I on behalf of the Tribunal thank you for having come here to give evidence. I apologise to you if you have been kept waiting for some time and if your testimony was prolonged for a few days, perhaps longer than you expected. And with that, I think I can ask the usher to escort you. Once more, thank you for having come here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. And I would like to thank everyone else in this courtroom. It wasn't difficult for me. A lot of time has passed, so there were a few things that, et cetera. I don't think I want to lie about anyone and I don't want -- I want to tell the truth and I shall always try to do so. I'm glad if I have satisfied you to a certain extent, and I regret that there were people who were the cause of this evil. And thank you and goodbye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And have a safe journey home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anything further before we can call it a day?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, the question of the witnesses. Your Honours should be -- I want to make sure that Your Honours have it. For Witness 7.165, who is the witness after the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. The next one is 7.46. No?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The one after that is 7.165. And Your Honours will -- it was put in front of Your Honours. But I want to make sure now that you have documents. This witness produced a diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is a diary that was written effectively about as contemporaneously as you can get shortly after his release in Manjaca. Therefore, I'm proposing to use that and indeed examine him from some of those entries in the diary. So that's why we've copied it for Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I assume that this has been already disclosed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It was disclosed to the Defence sometime ago. But just so that you understand, because it's a fuller account of -- he's going to deal with the incidents of suffocation and another incident, and it's a fuller account of that that appeared in his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, the real difficulty is this: Because we've got the week's break and because we won't be able to start the next witness and I don't know how long the first witness is going to take tomorrow - that's 7.65. He was asked for, as I understand it -- Mr. Ackerman, you'll recall we discussed it, didn't require his attendance at all but Madam Fauveau did, and there's no dispute about the killing. So if the reality is -- Ms. Richterova will be calling the witness and estimates that to call him in chief is something in the region of -- if there's no objection to leading and the rest, then will take something between an hour and an hour and a half. So let's say the first part of the session. If Madam Fauveau can finish her cross-examination within the second part, leaving the next witness to start for after the second break, I have no doubt that that -- this witness in chief is going to take the best part of a session, because he's got so much detail of what actually happened. So I therefore would like some indication given, if that's possible, first as to whether it's -- it's likely that his cross-examination will be concluded on the Friday. He gives no direct evidence against either accused. He's not going to say that he saw them in Manjaca -- or whether or not he's not going to finish, in which case he'll have to go for a week and whether that's a desirable attribute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as tomorrow's witness is concerned, I think that 45 minutes or one hour at the most will be sufficient for me. But obviously that depends on the examination-in-chief. As for as the Friday witness is concerned, I have no idea. I really couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's virtually impossible to -- for me to say that we can complete all examinations of both these witnesses by Friday at close of business. We haven't heard their direct. It has not happened yet that a witness has testified totally in accordance with their statements. There's always new material. And so it's just difficult to do. I -- if the Court wants to be safe and not have him gone in the midst of his testimony, then we shouldn't call him, 'cause that's the safe thing. But we did that with Judge Draganovic, and I don't think it caused any serious problem that he had to leave and come back. And this guy will have to leave and come back in any event, so it seems to me we get as far as we can and bring him back afterward if we have to. But if you don't want to break up his testimony, then I would say let's send him home tomorrow. It's up to you, Your Honour. I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know it's up to us, but the question is I -- there are several issues involved, and I would rather -- what's your preference, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I -- I don't have a particular preference at all. He's here. He arrived yesterday. I can certainly conclude his evidence in chief by Friday, unless there's a lot more cross-examination of the first witness tomorrow than I anticipate. So he can go back -- he can start and go back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because as I see it, I can hardly recall one single witness that we disposed of in just one session.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think we've had two so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. But it's the exception rather than the rule. This one, if he's got this diary -- I don't know. I'm not very optimistic that we could actually start and finish. And in that case, from the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What I'm not anxious to do, Your Honour is waste any time at all. I've had a look at the July schedule, and to my horror we're sitting something like ten days in the whole of July, which is just, if I may put it that way, ludicrous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. But we are not the only ones, you know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. I know. It's just as scheduling, it just beggars belief. However, so what I'm not anxious to do is to lose any time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, if you think that the course of justice would not be endangered in any way by having him returned to where he comes from, having started giving evidence, as we did with Judge Draganovic, after all, then we can proceed that way and we wouldn't have wasted a day. In any case, I mean the assumption is that if we send him straight away home now and bring him back after the end of next week, the expense from the cost -- cost to the Tribunal point of view --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- is not going to be --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. It's not the expense. It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. I'm not giving that any importance.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. The thing that concerns me, Your Honour, is this: It's becoming gradually apparent that the part of the Defence case, as being run by Mr. Ackerman, is that there is a great big conspiracy going on in Sanski Most, effectively orchestrated by AID. The witness lives in Sanski Most. He will be going back to Sanski Most. What I'm anxious not to have to happen is that we're then going to spend -- waste half an hour or so on a series of questions about who he's spoken to and who he's seen in Sanski Most and any changes to his evidence and the like. And that's -- that's what's concerning me at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman never -- never puts such questions. I've never heard him put such --
