utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Absolutely. I was just going to say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Absolutely. Not a single question about AID, who he's seen, and we waste 20 minutes thereabouts every single time there's a witness from Sanski Most. And that's what concerns me at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's never mentioned -- Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if I may try to facilitate your work. As you know, I'm all by myself still this week. I hope that I was cooperative, just like my client, who agreed to be represented by me only for a longer period. However, I seriously doubt that I shall be able to properly prepare the cross-examination of a third witness, if he comes on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Fauveau, let me say it in open court that this Chamber has not had for a single moment any reason, small or big, to doubt your cooperation. You have -- and that applies to Mr. Ackerman as well. You have been most cooperative. I must say that. However - however - we have to take a decision now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think, Ms. Korner, the -- this Chamber tends at not wasting Friday doing nothing. I mean, it's -- as you say --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, I wasn't -- I wasn't suggesting for one moment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. I know that. But I think we ought to bring this witness here on the first occasion, after we have disposed of the previous one, and he starts his evidence. And then we'll take it up from there, and he will return when necessary to continue and conclude his evidence if he needs to return. I think that's the best way. Otherwise we would be wasting another day, which -- we don't have anything else to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't -- well, we do, actually, Your Honour. But I -- can I just mention the outstanding matters that are not yet dealt with in the last remaining minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: First of all, Variant A and B. There's been a ruling in the Samac case. I can take it from that that it is now accepted that that document is admitted without us having to call further evidence to support its authenticity? Because Mr. Ackerman said that they were awaiting the ruling in the Samac case. There has been such a ruling. If -- if there is still the residual doubt that this is a document that was issued by the SDS and referred to in countless other documents, publications, speeches, well, then we will call all the evidence before Your Honour that was called in the Samac case. I'm merely listing now the issues that are still not resolved. Secondly, Your Honour, we still haven't resolved or haven't been told as to whether the redactions in the Rule 92 Banja Luka statement are acceptable. Third, we still have Mr. Ackerman's application to enter into evidence the transcript of a witness from a previous case. And we made brief submissions. But Mr. Ackerman, when I heard say last week when I objected to, I retain the objection, and I await with interest Mr. Ackerman's grounds for saying it's admissible or relevant or this case. I'm trying think, there was one other matter I've now lost it

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Dzonlic?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There is Mr. Dzonlic's documents. And I'm perfectly certain there are some other bits and pieces. But Your Honour, all those are still to the best of my recollection outstanding matters which ought to be dealt with at some stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. The Variant A and B, I don't know if you are in a position or prepared to make a statement now, today. If you're not, you will have time to do that. But we will need to know exactly where we stand so that if evidence needs to be brought forward, it will be brought forward without delay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There is an intervening fact -- and I don't want to make an argument based on the intervening fact until I have more knowledge. I'm told by a lawyer from the Bosanski Samac case that one of the things that developed during that was that the document had been -- had been originally handed to the Prosecutor by Alispahic who is the person who is the number one charged in Sarajevo with engaging in terrorist activities and things of that nature. Now, I don't know if that's true and I can't know if that's true until I look into it a little further. That's just information that I have. If that's true, it could affect how I feel about that document. With regard to the Rule 92 Banja Luka documents, I have no objection to them having been -- the changes that have been made to them. With regard to the transcript from the previous case, what I said in court when Ms. Korner was not here was that I believe that she wanted to argue that to Your Honours, and I therefore would not offer it without giving her the opportunity to argue against it. If Your Honours want to hear my basis for it being admitted, I'd be happy to tell you. With regard to the Dzonlic documents, I told you last week that I had decided to send them off to CLS for translation and would enter them as exhibits -- or seek to enter them as exhibits when they returned. So that's where I stand on all of those things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, first of all -- sorry, Your Honour. First of all, no, the onus is on Mr. Ackerman to show why a transcript of a -- of examination of a witness that's got nothing to do with this case relating to another person that's got nothing to do with this case should be admissible. It's not for me to. It's for him to justify it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I say so subject to correction. I may be completely confusing matters. But I am under the impression that when this matter arose, subsequently, as the -- your cross-examination progressed, it was more or less superseded by events. I mean, I got that impression. I don't know. I may be confusing matters. But I got the impression that at the end, you sort of abandoned the idea of needing -- and that you would reserve your position for later once you have verified some other events that you were referring to. I may be -- I may be completely going astray, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You're not. You're not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I think -- that's the impression that I formed in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You're not. And you've reminded me of, I think, exactly what I said about that. There's this whole -- there's this whole issue that is under investigation, both by the Prosecutor's Office and by us, regarding the AID issue. And I was last told by Mr. Cayley that there are about four boxes of material coming from Sarajevo regarding that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Will you be requesting an adjournment of two weeks, one month?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't think I'll need any adjournment at all. I'm satisfied the Prosecutor will provide us with whatever material is in those four boxes that is relevant to the credibility of any documents that might have come from AID. And so I'm awaiting that. I'm also frankly awaiting more information from Sarajevo about the nature of that case and what the exact charges are. As I understand it now, there has actually been no indictment filed yet. It's still in the early investigative stages. There are charges and five people are in jail, and I think that's as far as it's gone. And so I think -- I'm quite certain I'll be filing something with regard to that whole matter. But because of the way we're handling exhibits, we have until almost the last moment for the Court to determine how it's going to treat various exhibits. So it's not something that I think has to be dealt with immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. My recollection, Mr. Ackerman, I think actually when this evolved further, what happened was that first there was an agreement forthcoming from you that -- and at that moment you were still here present -- that you would postpone this till the -- towards the end of the testimony of the cross-examination -- or your cross-examination of that particular witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But towards the end. Then you came to the conclusion that there was no point in pushing any further your previous request for admitting -- having this transcript admitted, that you will maybe feel the need to do that again at some later point in time but obviously in reference to some other witness or some other evidence that you would bring over.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You're dead right. It is tied up with what I think may be a larger issue, and it doesn't bear consideration outside consideration of that larger issue. So let's leave it for the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Then one other thing -- one other matter which is outstanding, Ms. Korner, is the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- statement of the dead --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. We're waiting -- Your Honour, that's going to wait until after the Prijedor section, which will now be September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Because it relates to the witness who's going to come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just want to make it absolutely clear that that transcript doesn't even remotely begin to get entered as any kind of exhibit, whether it's a temporary acting exhibit, an unpaid exhibit, or whatever exhibit, until this has been argued, because I object to that in its entirety. Your Honour, as far as Mr. Dzonlic is concerned -- and I'm sorry, it may have been last week and I missed it -- so I understand that Mr. Ackerman is in fact going to enter all the documents we gave him as exhibits?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, I remember him stating that those will become Defence exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Fine. Okay. Well, in that case, otherwise we'd simply enter them ourselves. But I'm perfectly happy for it to go in through the Defence. And as far as the dead witness is concerned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The situation hasn't changed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- the situation will have to wait. And just -- I did say this once but perhaps I ought to remind Your Honours and the Defence. The next municipality will be Kljuc. The document -- the List of Documents is being prepared and I think will be given to the Defence this Friday before the break. And it may be that Your Honours will get the bundles as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you for providing us with that information now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. And Your Honour, we'll be doing the Rule 92 motion as well over the next week. Your Honour, what we are anxious to try and achieve, which is why I'm somewhat distressed about the few days we appear to be sitting in July with court maintenance and the like, is to complete Kljuc municipality by the end of July, by the time of the break, which I understand is the 26th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We still have -- Sanski Most you still have --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have three or four crime-based witnesses left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There is one witness -- and I can't remember his number -- who has got cancer and we're having inquiries made this week. Oh, I see that -- I wonder if I could borrow -- thank you. Your Honour, it's the witness number 7.59. It may be, Your Honour, that we'll have to try and do him through videolink. We're making inquiries this week to see whether he's fit to travel. But we should complete witnesses on the list numbers 27, 28, 29, 30, and 31 -- well, 32, Your Honour, I can just remind Your Honours has to testify on Friday, the 21st of July. So that's the week after we come back. I'm tempted to ask Your Honours to cancel the week's holiday, but I know that would cause a lot of problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 21st of July we will be changing -- I remember -- that's when we are changing the courtroom -- or no. 21st of July anyway. Yes. But we still have 14 witnesses here. Okay. Two of them are Rule 92?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. 21st of June. Did I say July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. June. No, Your Honour, we don't have 14 witnesses left. The ones at the bottom are Rule 92.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, the last two.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The last one certainly we -- yeah, we may -- I think we do. We have 12. Your Honour is right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have 12, plus two Rule 92.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And we've got BT21.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you have BT21.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we're going to try -- we're trying to get them through quickly. As I say -- [Microphone not activated] May I make this absolutely clear. Your Honours perfectly -- Your Honours are perfectly entitled to stop examination-in-chief --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Ms. Korner, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours are perfectly entitled to stop examination-in-chief if Your Honours have heard sufficient on a particular issue or if Your Honours feel that it's unnecessary to go any further. We can't second-guess what's in Your Honours' mind. So for example, Your Honours may feel you've heard enough about Manjaca but we don't know that. There's been no challenge to it but there's been general challenge to the credibility of the witnesses. So a number of these witnesses have been in Manjaca and are going to be saying the same things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's again -- saying there has been no challenge is not precise, because for example today the witness was questioned on the correctness or otherwise or the -- of statements made by Merhamet, statements made by Paddy Ashdown. So even the conditions are being contested. This is -- I don't think that there is anything in this case so far except for maybe a killing or two that has not been contested as a fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is problem. I mean --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But it's -- but Your Honours are -- in the end result, Your Honours can say -- because we can go on calling witnesses forever, and will if that's what's required to convince Your Honours that Manjaca was not a particularly pleasant place, to put it at its lowest. It's not just these witnesses, Your Honour. It's witnesses from Kljuc that we're going to hear, who went to the same place. It seems to me that yes, of course there is directly respond -- we hold -- no question about it, we allege that General Talic is directly responsible for not controlling the conditions in that camp. When I say there's been no challenge, there's been no challenge to individual beatings or killings or the like, because obviously there can't be. You know, it's not suggested that either of these two defendants, accused, directly participated in that. But Your Honour, we have to -- somebody has to somehow get a hold of, if you like, this case. We're trying, but one of the real problems is -- and Mr. Ackerman will have his say -- is that appreciating it's a document-heavy case, we have to go through the aspects of the case that are obviously part and parcel of the crime base. Cross-examination is exceedingly lengthy and sometimes, Your Honour, in our submission, doesn't go to the root of the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not comment -- going to comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But Your Honour, I'm saying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the case of this witness, for example, this last one, even the examination-in-chief was supposed to last a day, if I remember correctly, when you first started or indicated to us -- when I asked you how long did you expect -- well, it lasted double.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Your Honour, I said it would take just over a day, and it did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It lasted much more than a day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. It finished at the first break, or just after, in fact. Mr. Ackerman --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's today?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Today is Wednesday. It started on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. We continued yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You mean the whole -- Your Honour, I can only estimate examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. And so can we. I mean, we don't know. And this is the problem. Because the way the witness answers will very much condition then the whole examination-in-chief or the cross-examination. This witness, when I -- when I drew his attention, answer yes or no, we went much speedier and Madam Fauveau could finish her cross-examination in half of what she expected or she had told us it would last.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's the form of the -- it's the form of the question as well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, I know. I know, Ms. Korner. But I think what we need to do is that Prosecution should pick the best witnesses, say, on Manjaca. If you think that you have six, seven, eight key witnesses, describe from -- from Sanski Most who are in a position to provide the Trial Chamber with whatever you want to prove with regard to the conditions in Manjaca, you can stop there. But that's --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, then, Your Honour, I could stop now, because I've had two witnesses give evidence of what happened in Manjaca. The witness who's coming either tomorrow or Friday -- well, Your Honours, I would invite Your Honours to have a look at what's in the -- I say diary. It's more of a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. It has arrived now and we'll have to. Yes, Mr. Ackerman. Please don't be long so that we --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Korner said a lot of things, and I should have a right to respond to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I know. But if you want, you can have your time tomorrow so that we don't keep the staff here more than we promised they would stay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, then let's let them go, and I'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You will --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll depend on speaking with you first thing in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We'll deal with this first thing in the morning. I think that's better. Thank you. My apologies to the technical staff and to the interpreters. Yes. I wanted to announce that there is a further change again, because the changes in Milosevic and changes in Simic and we will have to move back to Courtroom I tomorrow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
